**Introduction and Dataset**  
**Project Objective**  
The goal of this project is to analyze the effectiveness of different dimensionality reduction techniques, including PCA (Principal Component Analysis), and LDA (Linear Discriminant Analysis). By reducing the dimensions of the breast cancer diagnosis dataset, only the variables with the highest weight in determining whether a patient has a cancerous tumor or a benign tumor will be shown and used. This will ultimately show the most determining variables that indicate cancer in a patient or not. PCA and LDA are being compared to show different methods of dimensionality reduction, and which one proves to be the most accurate and reliable for future use cases. By using dimensionality reduction, breast cancer identifiers can be easier to spot, because instead of looking for several different conditions or identifiers in a patient, only a few need to be checked on, since those few variables provide the best indicators as to whether a patient has breast cancer or not.

**Dataset Description**  
Dataset: Breast Cancer Wisconsin Dataset  
Link: [https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/uciml/breast-cancer-wisconsin-data?](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/uciml/breast-cancer-wisconsin-data?)  
Size of Dataset: 569 samples, 30 numerical features  
Target Classes: The two target classes used in the dataset are malignant and benign. Malignant is defined as patients with cancerous tumors that can spread throughout the body and may even cause death. Benign patients are patients with tumors that are non-cancerous, and grow very slowly, meaning they are not as malignant or harmful, and are less likely to be deadly.  
Class Distribution: The class distribution of the dataset is around 37% malignant, and around 63% benign.  
![][image1]

**Feature Understanding**  
Mean Features (Average Measurements)

- mean\_radius — Mean (average) tumor radius  
- mean\_texture — Mean (average) texture  
- mean\_perimeter — Mean (average) perimeter  
- mean\_area — Mean (average) area  
- mean\_smoothness — Mean (average) smoothness  
- mean\_compactness — Mean (average) compactness  
- mean\_concavity — Mean (average) concavity  
- mean\_concave\_points — Mean (average) concave points  
- mean\_symmetry — Mean (average) symmetry  
- mean\_fractal\_dimension — Mean (average) fractal dimension

Standard Error (SE) Features (Measurement Variability)

- radius\_error — Standard Error (SE) of radius  
- texture\_error — Standard Error (SE) of texture  
- perimeter\_error — Standard Error (SE) of perimeter  
- area\_error — Standard Error (SE) of area  
- smoothness\_error — Standard Error (SE) of smoothness  
- compactness\_error — Standard Error (SE) of compactness  
- concavity\_error — Standard Error (SE) of concavity  
- concave\_points\_error — Standard Error (SE) of concave points  
- symmetry\_error — Standard Error (SE) of symmetry  
- fractal\_dimension\_error — Standard Error (SE) of fractal dimension

Worst Features (Maximum / Extreme Values)

- worst\_radius — Worst (maximum) radius  
- worst\_texture — Worst (maximum) texture  
- worst\_perimeter — Worst (maximum) perimeter  
- worst\_area — Worst (maximum) area  
- worst\_smoothness — Worst (maximum) smoothness  
- worst\_compactness — Worst (maximum) compactness  
- worst\_concavity — Worst (maximum) concavity  
- worst\_concave\_points — Worst (maximum) concave points  
- worst\_symmetry — Worst (maximum) symmetry  
- worst\_fractal\_dimension — Worst (maximum) fractal dimension

| Measurement | Explanation | What it tells us biologically |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Radius | Distance from the center to the edge of the tumor | Tumor Size |
| Texture | Variations in gray-scale pixel intensity  | Cell consistency (uniform vs irregular) |
| Perimeter | Length around the tumor boundary | Tumor size/shape complexity |
| Area | Total area of tumor | Overall tumor size |
| Smoothness | How smooth the edges are | Irregular growth patterns |
| Compactness | How tightly packed the tumor is | Density of tumor cells |
| Concavity | Depth of inward curves in boundary | Malignant tumors often have deep indentations |
| Concave Points | Number of concave regions | More points leads to more irregular tumor |
| Symmetry | Balance of tumor shape | Cancer tumors are often asymmetric |
| Fractal Dimension | Complexity of boundary | Higher \= more chaotic/irregular shape |

**Key Insights**

1. Feature Separation Between Classes:

Malignant tumors tend to have higher values for features like mean\_radius, mean\_perimeter, and mean\_area compared to benign tumors. The boxplots show clear differences, meaning these features help distinguish between the two classes.

2. Highly Correlated Features (\>0.8):

Features such as radius, perimeter, and area are strongly correlated (above 0.8). This means they provide similar information, showing some redundancy in the dataset and supporting the use of dimensionality reduction.

3. Outliers in Tumor Measurements:

Outliers appear in features like area, perimeter, and concavity, especially for malignant tumors. These represent unusually large or irregular tumors.

4. Distribution Patterns:

Many features, like area and perimeter, are right-skewed, meaning most values are smaller with a few very large ones. This shows the data is not normally distributed.

5. Class Distribution:

The dataset has more benign cases (\~63%) than malignant (\~37%), showing a slight imbalance, but it is not extreme.

**Data Preprocessing**

**Missing Values**  
![][image3]  
Because no missing values were present, no action was taken.

**Feature Scaling**  
Because different features had different magnitudes (like mean\_area having values 1000+ but mean\_radius having values 10-20), different features were given different weights. Before scaling, features with higher magnitudes are by default given more weight simply because they are higher in value. Scaling is important to make PCA and LDA algorithms more accurate because both algorithms base their formulas based on magnitude and variance. Because certain features have higher magnitudes, they are given more weight in PCA and LDA. After scaling however, all features are given the same importance and weight, and from there, only the features that have the highest effect on determining tumor type are used.

Before vs after scaling:  
![][image19]  
Before scaling, features like mean\_area are in the thousands range, but features like mean\_smoothness are in the decimals range. After scaling, both features are between \-1 and 1 based on how far they are from the mean of that feature.

**Train-Test Split**  
![][image20]  
The train test split used in the project was a 80 \- 20 split. After testing with both a 70-30 split, and a 90-10 split, the 80-20 split proved to have the highest overall scores in the performance table. As a result, the 80-20 train-test split was used. It was stratified to maintain the class balance for the target variable, and the random\_state was set to 42 for reproducibility. The training set size had 455 samples, while the testing set size had 114 samples.  
**Principal Component Analysis**

**PCA Concept Understanding**  
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a dimensionality reduction technique that transforms the original features into a smaller set of new variables called principal components. These components are created in a way that captures the maximum amount of variance in the data. PCA is an unsupervised method, meaning it does not use the target labels (malignant or benign) when reducing dimensions. Instead, it focuses only on the structure of the data itself. By preserving the directions of highest variance, PCA keeps the most important information while reducing the number of features.

**Optimal Components**  
Scree Plot:  
![][image21]  
The scree plot shows that after the first 6-7 principal components, the explained variance for the following components is very minimal, and won’t have much of an effect on deciding which class the patient should fall under. Therefore, more than about 10 principal components should not be used.

Cumulative Variance Plot:  
![][image22]

Table of Variance by Component  
**![][image23]**  
**![][image24]**

The optimal k chosen was k \= 10, since after k=10, 95% of the variance was explained, meaning that after k=10, each principal component had minimal variance and meaning as for contributing to the separation of classes. k \=10 didn’t oversegment the dataset, but also wasn’t too broad and included 95% of the variance in the dataset.

**PCA Implementation**  
The final number of components specified and used was 10 components (k=10). The variance explained by PC1 and PC2 was 62.69%. This means that based on just PC1 and PC2, 62.69% of the variance in the dataset is accounted for, meaning that PCA effectively reduced a 30 dimensional dataset into a 2D dataset, while retaining 62.69% accuracy.  
![][image25]

**2D/3D Visualizations**  
2D Scatter Plot:  
![][image26]

3D Scatterplot:  
![][image27]

**Feature Combinations**  
PC1 mainly represents tumor shape irregularity, as it is strongly influenced by concavity and concave point features. These features describe how uneven or indented the tumor boundary is, which is a key indicator of malignancy.

PC2 represents variation in boundary complexity and texture, as it is influenced by fractal dimension and error-based features. This component captures more subtle differences in tumor structure rather than overall shape.

**Optimization**  
After trying out multiple k values, k=10 proved to be the best choice. If a value for k under 10 was chosen, then the total variance explained by the number of principal components would be less than 95%, making the model less accurate and reliable overall. k values above 10 proved to be very insignificantly better than k=10, and would over segment the dataset and reduce the benefits of using dimensionality reduction. Therefore, the best choice that was the most efficient, beneficial, and inclusive, was k=10.  
![][image28]  
**Linear Discriminant Analysis**

**LDA Concept Understanding:**  
Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) is a dimensionality reduction technique that transforms the original features into new components that best separate the classes. Unlike PCA, LDA is a supervised method, meaning it uses the target labels (malignant and benign) when reducing dimensions. LDA works by maximizing the separation between classes while minimizing variation within each class, making it especially useful for classification. The number of components LDA can produce is limited by the formula n\_classes − 1, so for this dataset with two classes, LDA can only create one component.

**LDA Constraints**  
For binary classification problems, Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) can produce a maximum of 1 component. This is because the number of components is limited by the formula n\_classes − 1\. Since this dataset has 2 classes (malignant and benign), the maximum number of components is:

2 − 1 \= 1

This means LDA can only reduce the data to a single dimension while still maximizing class separation. This is different from PCA, which does not depend on the number of classes and can produce multiple components based on the number of features.

**LDA Implementation**  
Because LDA uses n\_classes \- 1, only 1 LDA component could be made (which is the max for binary classification). LDA accounts for 100% of the variation, meaning that the line of separation created by the LDA algorithm was inclusive of 100% of the class separation data. The model also properly uses class labels by distinguishing between malignant and benign.

**1D Visualization**  
![][image29]  
![][image30]  
The separation quality of the LDA algorithm was very high. Little to no overlaps were seen between the malignant and benign classes, meaning that LDA was very effective in separating the classes based on one LDA component.

**Feature Contributions**  
The top features contributing to the LDA model, based on coefficient magnitude, are mean\_radius (13.506), worst\_area (11.273), mean\_compactness (5.332), concavity\_error (2.543), and perimeter\_error (2.099). These coefficients show how strongly each feature influences the LDA component, with larger values indicating greater importance in separating the classes. The discriminant axis (LD1) mainly reflects differences in tumor size and structure. Features like mean\_radius and worst\_area represent tumor size, while compactness and concavity-related features describe shape irregularity. This shows that larger and more irregular tumors are key factors in distinguishing malignant from benign cases.

**Optimizations**  
For LDA, optimization options are limited because binary classification allows only one component (n\_classes − 1 \= 1), so there are no additional dimensions to tune. However, proper preprocessing is still important, and StandardScaler was applied to all features to ensure that differences in magnitude did not bias the model. The resulting LD1 projection shows strong separation between malignant and benign classes, with most values forming distinct groups. Although there is some overlap, the overall separation is clear, indicating that LDA effectively distinguishes between the two classes.  
**PCA vs LDA Comparison**

**Visual Comparison**  
![][image31]

**Quantitative Comparison**

Comparison Table:

| Feature | PCA (Principal Component Analysis) | LDA (Linear Discriminant Analysis) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Type of Method | Unsupervised | Supervised |
| Uses Target Labels | No | Yes |
| Main Goal | Maximize variance in data | Maximize separation between classes |
| Focus | Captures overall data patterns | Focuses on class differences |
| Number of Components | Up to number of features (30) | Limited to n\_classes − 1 |
| Max Components (This Dataset) | 30 | 1 (2 − 1 \= 1\) |
| Explained Variance | Measures total data variance | Measures class separation |
| Explained Variance (This Project) | \~95% with 10 components | 100% with 1 component |
| Dimensionality Reduction | Flexible (choose k) | Very limited |
| Visualization | 2D and 3D possible | Only 1D for binary classification |
| Separation Quality | Moderate (some overlap) | Stronger separation |
| Best Use Case  | Data compression, visualization | Classification tasks |

Classification Performance Table:  
![][image32]

**Analysis and Insights**  
Overall, the model using the original dataset performed best, but between the dimensionality reduction methods, LDA performs slightly better than PCA for classification tasks because it is designed to maximize class separation. PCA’s main strength is that it effectively reduces dimensionality while preserving most of the data’s variance, making it useful for visualization and noise reduction. However, since PCA does not use class labels, it may not always provide the best separation for classification. In contrast, LDA uses class labels to create components that separate groups, which improves classification performance, but it is limited in the number of components it can produce, especially for binary datasets. Therefore, PCA is best used for data compression and visualization, while LDA is more suitable for classification problems, such as medical diagnosis, where distinguishing between classes is critical.  
**Findings and Conclusion**

**Key Findings**  
The most important features were identified based on their contributions to PC1, PC2, and the LDA component (LD1). Features related to tumor size and shape, such as radius, area, compactness, concavity, and concave points, had the highest influence across both PCA and LDA. The optimal number of principal components was determined to be k \= 10, as it preserves approximately 95% of the total variance while significantly reducing dimensionality. Both PCA and LDA were effective in reducing the number of features, but LDA showed stronger class separation, making it more suitable for cancer diagnosis. Overall, dimensionality reduction helped simplify the dataset while maintaining high classification performance, demonstrating its usefulness in medical applications.

**Conclusion**  
This project successfully applied PCA and LDA to reduce the dimensionality of the breast cancer dataset while maintaining strong classification performance. Both methods were effective, but LDA is recommended as the better technique for this problem because it provides stronger class separation and is specifically designed for classification tasks. PCA is still useful for reducing dimensionality and visualizing data, but it does not use class labels, which can limit its effectiveness for classification. These results have important practical implications for medical diagnosis, as dimensionality reduction can simplify complex datasets while still allowing accurate identification of malignant and benign tumors. Overall, this project demonstrates a strong understanding of how dimensionality reduction techniques can be used to improve data analysis and support real-world decision-making.

**Future Work**  
Several improvements could be made to extend this project. First, nonlinear dimensionality reduction techniques such as t-SNE and UMAP could be applied to better capture complex patterns in the data that PCA and LDA may miss. Second, the model could be tested on additional medical datasets to evaluate how well these techniques generalize to other types of cancer or diseases. Third, more advanced methods such as deep learning models (e.g., neural networks) could be used to improve classification performance. Finally, feature selection techniques could be applied before dimensionality reduction to remove less important variables and further improve efficiency.
